title: Abstraction studio
subject: Abstraction
mission: Choose the details a school equipment-loan system needs. Explain what can be left out and why.
donow: Would a photograph always be more useful than a simple map?
outcomes: Select details for a stated purpose.
Justify why some details can be ignored.
starter: A pupil needs to find the library. Which is more useful: a map of corridors or a list of wall colours? Explain.
starter_answer: A corridor map shows routes and destinations. Wall colours are usually unnecessary for finding a route.
terms: Keeping relevant details and removing unnecessary detail for a particular purpose.
A simplified representation of a real system.

stations.name: Keep the purpose
facts: Start with the problem to solve.
Relevant details depend on the purpose.
A simpler model can still be useful.
stations.challenge: Why can a map omit carpet patterns?
stations.answer: Carpet patterns do not help identify a route to the library.

tasks.q: Which detail belongs on a route map?
tasks.fb: Connections between rooms

tasks.q: For recognising a camera icon, which detail is least necessary?
tasks.fb: The exact serial number. Start with the problem to solve.

stations.info: Carpet patterns do not help identify a route to the library.

stations.name: Essential information
facts: A loan system must identify the borrower.
It must identify the borrowed item.
It needs enough data to track the loan.
stations.challenge: Name two details needed to track a camera loan.
stations.answer: Borrower ID and item ID identify who has which camera. The due date helps track returns.

tasks.q: Classify details for tracking loans.
tasks.fb: Keep details that support identifying and returning the item.

tasks.q: Which detail helps identify an overdue loan?
tasks.fb: Due date. A loan system must identify the borrower.

stations.info: Borrower ID and item ID identify who has which camera. The due date helps track returns.

stations.name: Remove distractions
facts: Not every real-world detail belongs in a model.
Removing detail makes a model easier to use.
Do not remove information needed for accuracy.
stations.challenge: Why might an icon omit the serial number?
stations.answer: Its purpose is to recognise a camera category. A serial number identifies one particular camera.

tasks.q: What would damage a route map?
tasks.fb: Removing the corridor connections

tasks.q: Removing required corridor links is...
tasks.fb: Too much simplification. Not every real-world detail belongs in a model.

stations.info: Its purpose is to recognise a camera category. A serial number identifies one particular camera.

stations.name: Purpose changes relevance
facts: A detail can matter in one task and not another.
A repair system needs different data from a route map.
Explain choices using the stated task.
stations.challenge: When would a room light fault become relevant?
stations.answer: When planning repairs, the fault and room location help staff repair the correct light.

tasks.q: Match purpose to a useful detail.
tasks.fb: Each detail supports a particular decision.

tasks.q: A fault description becomes relevant when...
tasks.fb: Planning repairs. A detail can matter in one task and not another.

stations.info: When planning repairs, the fault and room location help staff repair the correct light.

stations.name: Abstraction in software
facts: Users can work without knowing every internal detail.
A button can hide several processing steps.
The hidden steps still happen.
stations.challenge: What does a return button hide from its user?
stations.answer: It hides the detailed steps for finding the loan and updating its stored status.

tasks.q: A return button is an abstraction because it...
a: Hides internal steps behind one clear action
tasks.fb: Hides internal steps behind one clear action

tasks.q: Hiding processing behind a button means...
a: Users need not manage every internal step
tasks.fb: Users need not manage every internal step. Users can work without knowing every internal detail.

stations.info: It hides the detailed steps for finding the loan and updating its stored status.

stations.name: Evaluate a model
facts: Check whether the model solves the problem.
Add missing relevant details.
Remove detail that only distracts.
stations.challenge: How should this route map be improved?
stations.answer: Add the connections between rooms so users can plan a route. Textures can be removed.

tasks.q: Which justification is strongest?
a: Keep due dates so overdue loans can be identified
tasks.fb: Keep due dates so overdue loans can be identified

tasks.q: A model should be judged against...
tasks.fb: Its stated purpose. Check whether the model solves the problem.

stations.info: Add the connections between rooms so users can plan a route. Textures can be removed.

final.q: Choose data for identifying overdue equipment loans.
final.fb: The system needs to identify the loan and whether its due date has passed.

final.q: Why is abstraction useful here?
a: It reduces unnecessary detail while preserving what the task needs
It removes the need to test
final.fb: It reduces unnecessary detail while preserving what the task needs

plenary: Define abstraction. [2]
Keep relevant detail (1) and remove unnecessary detail for a purpose (1).
A delivery map omits the colour of each house. Explain why this is appropriate. [2]
The map is used to find routes (1). House colours are not needed to represent the route connections (1).
Give one detail that a loan system should retain and justify it. [2]
Borrower ID identifies who has the item, or due date supports identifying overdue items. One suitable detail (1) with a linked reason (1).

title: Model design lab
subject: Applying abstraction
mission: Build and test simple models. Select the data needed to compare locations and calculate fares.
donow: Can a simplified model give a correct answer?
outcomes: Apply abstraction to a new problem.
Refine a model when requirements change.
starter: A program compares two places north or south. Does it need latitude, shop names or building colours?
starter_answer: Latitude is relevant to north/south position. Shop names and building colours are not.

stations.name: Define the question
facts: A model answers a specific question.
Write the required output first.
Then decide which inputs are necessary.
stations.challenge: Why define the output before selecting data?
stations.answer: The required answer determines which data the model needs.

tasks.q: Which input supports a north/south comparison?
tasks.fb: Latitude

tasks.q: The required output helps determine...
tasks.fb: Which inputs are relevant. A model answers a specific question.

stations.info: The required answer determines which data the model needs.

stations.name: Signed coordinates
facts: Northern latitudes are positive.
Southern latitudes are negative.
A larger latitude is further north.
stations.challenge: Which is further north: -8 or -21? Explain.
stations.answer: -8 is larger than -21, so it is further north.

tasks.q: Which latitude is further north?
tasks.fb: -3 is the greatest value, so it is furthest north.

tasks.q: Which is further north: -15 or -4?
tasks.fb: -4. Northern latitudes are positive.

stations.info: -8 is larger than -21, so it is further north.

stations.name: Equality matters
facts: Two values can be equal.
A two-way comparison may miss this case.
Specify an output for every valid case.
stations.challenge: Why is an equality case needed?
stations.answer: Without it, equal latitudes could be incorrectly labelled north or south.

tasks.q: A = 12 and B = 12. What should be output?
tasks.fb: Same latitude

tasks.q: Which comparison checks equal values?
tasks.fb: A == B. Two values can be equal.

stations.info: Without it, equal latitudes could be incorrectly labelled north or south.

stations.name: Inputs and processing
facts: Inputs supply the data.
Processes transform or compare it.
Outputs communicate the result.
stations.challenge: Classify multiplying distance by 2.
stations.answer: It is a process because it transforms the input into the fare.

tasks.q: Classify each part of the fare model.
tasks.fb: Input enters, a process calculates, and output leaves the system.

tasks.q: A displayed fare is...
tasks.fb: Output. Inputs supply the data.

stations.info: It is a process because it transforms the input into the fare.

stations.name: Change the requirement
facts: A new requirement may need new data.
Review the model before adding detail.
Keep the change relevant to the new purpose.
stations.challenge: What extra coordinate supports east/west comparison?
stations.answer: Longitude supports comparing east/west positions within a stated coordinate convention.

tasks.q: A fare now depends on passenger age. What changes?
a: Add age as an input and a discount rule
tasks.fb: Add age as an input and a discount rule

tasks.q: Which input supports an age discount?
tasks.fb: Passenger age. A new requirement may need new data.

stations.info: Longitude supports comparing east/west positions within a stated coordinate convention.

stations.name: Test the simplified model
facts: Use examples with known answers.
Include less obvious cases.
Refine the rules if an example fails.
stations.challenge: Why test equal and negative latitudes?
stations.answer: They check equality and signed-number comparisons that positive unequal examples may miss.

tasks.q: Order the model-development steps.
tasks.fb: Test against the original question.

tasks.q: Which case checks equality?
tasks.fb: 8 and 8. Use examples with known answers.

stations.info: They check equality and signed-number comparisons that positive unequal examples may miss.

final.q: A fare is distance * 2. Distance is 7. What is output?
Match each improvement to its purpose.
final.fb: Only add detail that supports the requirement.

plenary: Identify input, process and output for a fare calculated as distance multiplied by 2. [3]
Distance (1), multiply by 2 (1), fare (1).
Explain why comparing only positive latitudes is insufficient testing. [2]
It misses negative values (1), where incorrect use of absolute values could reverse the result (1).
A model compares only north/south locations. Explain a refinement needed for equal latitudes. [2]
Add a test for equality (1) and output a same-latitude result (1).

title: Decomposition workshop
subject: Decomposition and structure diagrams
mission: Break an equipment-loan system into manageable parts and build a structure diagram.
donow: How could a team share the work of building one program?
starter: A school club needs to register members, lend equipment and record returns. Name three smaller problems.
starter_answer: Manage members, issue loans and process returns are three suitable sub-problems.
terms: Breaking a problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems.
A hierarchy showing a system and its component sub-problems.

stations.name: Split the problem
facts: Start with the whole task.
Identify separate responsibilities.
Break large parts down further.
stations.challenge: Suggest three parts of a library system.
stations.answer: Manage members, issue books and process returned books are suitable parts.

tasks.q: Which example is decomposition?
a: Split a shop into stock, orders and payments
Put every instruction in one block
tasks.fb: Split a shop into stock, orders and payments

tasks.q: Which is a sub-problem of a loan system?
tasks.fb: Process a return. Start with the whole task.

stations.info: Manage members, issue books and process returned books are suitable parts.

stations.name: Read the hierarchy
facts: The top box is the whole system.
Child boxes are parts of their parent.
Lower levels show more detail.
stations.challenge: What are the two parts of Issue loan?
stations.answer: Check availability and record borrower.

tasks.q: What does a line to a child box mean?
a: The child is a component of the parent
The child is an output value
tasks.fb: The child is a component of the parent

tasks.q: The top box of a structure diagram is...
tasks.fb: The complete system. The top box is the whole system.

stations.info: Check availability and record borrower.

stations.name: Refine a sub-problem
facts: Refinement adds useful detail.
Stop when each task is clear enough to solve.
Keep the hierarchy logically grouped.
stations.challenge: Break Process return into three smaller tasks.
stations.answer: Find the active loan, mark it returned and make the item available again.

tasks.q: Order a sensible refinement process.
steps: Check the parts cover the requirements
tasks.fb: Refinement adds detail to a decomposition.

tasks.q: Refinement means...
a: Breaking a large part into clearer smaller tasks
tasks.fb: Breaking a large part into clearer smaller tasks. Refinement adds useful detail.

stations.info: Find the active loan, mark it returned and make the item available again.

stations.name: Structure versus flow
facts: Structure diagrams show parts.
Flowcharts show execution and decisions.
A hierarchy does not specify run order.
stations.challenge: Why is a structure diagram not a flowchart?
stations.answer: It shows what the system contains, rather than the order of execution and decision paths.

tasks.q: Classify the diagram features.
tasks.fb: Do not read a hierarchy as execution order.

tasks.q: Does left-to-right position in a structure diagram define execution order?
a: Only if the boxes are blue
tasks.fb: No. Structure diagrams show parts.

stations.info: It shows what the system contains, rather than the order of execution and decision paths.

stations.name: Work as a team
facts: Smaller tasks can be allocated to people.
Parts can be tested separately.
Interfaces between parts must still agree.
stations.challenge: Why must both programmers agree on member ID?
stations.answer: Their parts exchange member details. A consistent ID allows the parts to work together.

tasks.q: Which is a benefit of decomposition?
a: Individual parts are easier to understand and test
tasks.fb: Individual parts are easier to understand and test

tasks.q: A shared interface helps parts...
tasks.fb: Exchange data consistently. Smaller tasks can be allocated to people.

stations.info: Their parts exchange member details. A consistent ID allows the parts to work together.

stations.name: Check coverage
facts: Compare the parts with the requirements.
Look for missing responsibilities.
Avoid duplicate or unclear tasks.
stations.challenge: Which responsibility is missing?
stations.answer: Processing returns is missing and must be included.

tasks.q: The system must report overdue loans. What should be added?
a: Nothing because all systems report automatically
tasks.fb: An overdue-report sub-problem

tasks.q: An omitted return function is found by checking...
tasks.fb: The decomposition against the requirements. Compare the parts with the requirements.

stations.info: Processing returns is missing and must be included.

final.q: Match each sub-problem to a suitable smaller task.
final.fb: Each child must belong to its parent.

final.q: Why test each part before combining them?
a: It helps locate faults within smaller sections
It proves the whole system cannot fail
It removes the need for shared data
final.fb: It helps locate faults within smaller sections

plenary: Define decomposition. [2]
Break a complex problem (1) into smaller manageable sub-problems (1).
Draw a structure diagram for a club system with members, loans and returns. Decompose loans into two tasks. [4]
Whole system above three appropriate parts (1), correct parent-child connections (1), check availability beneath loans (1), record loan beneath loans (1).
Explain one advantage of decomposition for a team. [2]
Separate tasks can be assigned to different people (1), allowing work on manageable parts in parallel (1).

title: Algorithm planning room
subject: Algorithmic thinking: sequence
mission: Design precise steps for issuing an equipment loan, then check their order and outputs.
donow: Why can instructions that seem obvious to a person confuse a computer?
starter: Put these actions in order: display total, input price, calculate total.
starter_answer: Input price, calculate total, display total.
terms: A finite set of precise steps for solving a problem.
Executing instructions in their stated order.

stations.name: A clear goal
facts: Algorithmic thinking plans a solution as steps.
State what must be achieved.
Check that the steps reach that goal.
stations.challenge: Why state the goal before writing steps?
stations.answer: The goal defines what counts as a correct result.

tasks.q: Algorithmic thinking involves...
a: Planning precise steps to solve a problem
tasks.fb: Planning precise steps to solve a problem

tasks.q: A useful algorithm must...
a: Reach the stated goal through precise steps
tasks.fb: Reach the stated goal through precise steps. Algorithmic thinking plans a solution as steps.

stations.info: The goal defines what counts as a correct result.

stations.name: Input, process, output
facts: Identify data entering the algorithm.
Identify operations on the data.
Identify the result to communicate.
stations.challenge: Name the inputs for calculating hire cost.
stations.answer: The number of hours and the hourly rate.

tasks.q: Classify the hire steps.
tasks.fb: The calculation is the process.

tasks.q: Multiplying hours by rate is...
tasks.fb: Processing. Identify data entering the algorithm.

stations.info: The number of hours and the hourly rate.

stations.name: Order matters
facts: A value must be available before use.
Calculate before displaying the result.
Changing order can change behaviour.
stations.challenge: What is wrong with printing total first?
stations.answer: The total has not yet been calculated from the inputs.

tasks.q: Order a total-cost algorithm.
tasks.fb: Read both values before calculating.

tasks.q: Which must happen before outputting a calculated total?
tasks.fb: Calculate the total. A value must be available before use.

stations.info: The total has not yet been calculated from the inputs.

stations.name: Remove ambiguity
facts: Instructions need clear actions and quantities.
Avoid words such as some or enough.
Specify what happens in each case.
stations.challenge: Rewrite Add some bonus points precisely.
stations.answer: Add 5 bonus points to score is one precise example.

tasks.q: Which instruction is precise?
tasks.fb: Increase score by 2

tasks.q: Which word often makes an instruction ambiguous?
tasks.fb: Some. Instructions need clear actions and quantities.

stations.info: Add 5 bonus points to score is one precise example.

stations.name: Follow the steps
facts: Trace an algorithm in its exact order.
Use the current value of a variable.
Assignment replaces its previous value.
stations.challenge: What is printed? Show the intermediate value.
stations.answer: x becomes 7 and then 14, so 14 is printed.

tasks.q: For x = 5, then x = x + 2, then x = x * 3, what is x?
x = 3; x = x + 4; x = x * 2. Output?
tasks.fb: 14. Trace an algorithm in its exact order.

stations.info: x becomes 7 and then 14, so 14 is printed.

stations.name: Check the result
facts: Use a simple example with a known answer.
Compare expected and actual results.
Correct the steps when they differ.
stations.challenge: How should the wrong rule be corrected?
stations.answer: Multiply quantity by price. Adding gives 7, not the expected 12.

tasks.q: A total is wrong. What is the useful next step?
a: Trace each calculation using known inputs
Change all variable names at random
tasks.fb: Trace each calculation using known inputs

tasks.q: 3 items cost 4 each. Why is output 7 wrong?
tasks.fb: It adds instead of multiplying. Use a simple example with a known answer.

stations.info: Multiply quantity by price. Adding gives 7, not the expected 12.

final.q: Put a simple loan algorithm in order.
steps: Read borrower ID and item ID
final.fb: The check must happen before recording the loan.

final.q: What is the charge for 4 hours at 3 per hour?

plenary: Explain algorithmic thinking. [2]
Plan a logical sequence of steps (1) that solves a stated problem (1).
Write an algorithm to input length and width and output area. [3]
Input length and width (1), area = length * width (1), output area (1).
Explain why the order of instructions matters. [2]
Later instructions can depend on earlier results (1), so using a result before calculation can be incorrect (1).

title: Decision control centre
subject: Algorithmic thinking: selection
mission: Build decisions that handle thresholds, equal values and combined conditions correctly.
donow: Is age greater than 16 the same as age at least 16?
starter: A club accepts pupils aged 12 or older. Should age 12 be accepted?
starter_answer: Yes. Age 12 is included, so the condition must be age >= 12.
terms: Choosing which instructions to execute using a condition.
An expression evaluated as true or false.

stations.name: Two possible paths
facts: A condition selects a path.
IF handles the true case.
ELSE handles the false case.
stations.challenge: What happens when available is false?
stations.answer: The ELSE branch prints Unavailable.

tasks.q: If available is false, which message is printed?
tasks.fb: Unavailable

tasks.q: An IF condition evaluates to...
tasks.fb: True or false. A condition selects a path.

stations.info: The ELSE branch prints Unavailable.

stations.name: Include the boundary
facts: Greater than excludes equality.
Greater than or equal includes equality.
Match the condition to the rule.
stations.challenge: Why does age > 12 not match the rule?
stations.answer: It rejects a pupil aged exactly 12, although the rule includes them.

tasks.q: Which condition means score is at least 50?
tasks.fb: score >= 50

tasks.q: Which age is excluded by age > 12 but included by age >= 12?
tasks.fb: 12. Greater than excludes equality.

stations.info: It rejects a pupil aged exactly 12, although the rule includes them.

stations.name: Three-way decisions
facts: Some problems need more than two outcomes.
Check greater, less and equal cases.
Each valid input should have an outcome.
stations.challenge: What happens if the draw case is omitted?
stations.answer: Equal values may get the wrong result or no intended output.

tasks.q: A = 7 and B = 7. What is the correct result?
tasks.fb: Draw

tasks.q: Which result fits a = 9 and b = 4?
tasks.fb: A wins. Some problems need more than two outcomes.

stations.info: Equal values may get the wrong result or no intended output.

stations.name: Both conditions
facts: AND is true when both conditions are true.
Use it when both requirements must hold.
Check each requirement separately.
stations.challenge: Can this member borrow the unavailable item?
stations.answer: No. Both membership and availability are required, and availability is false.

tasks.q: Which permits a loan only if both checks pass?
tasks.fb: member AND available

tasks.q: true AND false is...
tasks.fb: False. AND is true when both conditions are true.

stations.info: No. Both membership and availability are required, and availability is false.

stations.name: Either condition
facts: OR is true when at least one condition is true.
It is also true when both are true.
Do not confuse OR with exactly one.
stations.challenge: Does a person who meets both conditions qualify?
stations.answer: Yes. OR includes the case where both conditions are true.

tasks.q: student = false, senior = true. What is student OR senior?
tasks.fb: True

tasks.q: true OR true is...
tasks.fb: True. OR is true when at least one condition is true.

stations.info: Yes. OR includes the case where both conditions are true.

stations.name: Nested decisions
facts: A decision can sit inside another decision.
The outer path controls whether it is reached.
Indentation helps show the structure.
stations.challenge: If member is false, is the inner decision reached?
stations.answer: No. The outer IF body is skipped.

tasks.q: Which describes nesting?
a: Changing an input to an output
tasks.fb: Placing one selection inside another

tasks.q: An inner branch inside a false outer IF is...
tasks.fb: Skipped. A decision can sit inside another decision.

stations.info: No. The outer IF body is skipped.

final.q: Match the phrase to its condition.
final.fb: Equality must be handled as the wording requires.

final.q: A loan needs a member AND an available item. Member is true and available is false. Result?
final.fb: Reject the loan

plenary: Write a condition for a temperature from 18 to 24 inclusive. [2]
temperature >= 18 (1) AND temperature <= 24 (1).
Explain the difference between AND and OR. [2]
AND needs both conditions true (1). OR needs at least one true (1).
An algorithm uses age > 16 for a rule of at least 16. Identify and correct the error. [2]
The boundary age 16 is rejected (1). Use age >= 16 (1).

title: Loop planning lab
subject: Algorithmic thinking: iteration
mission: Plan repetition that counts accurately and terminates. Combine loops with decisions.
donow: How could a program process 100 loans without writing the same instructions 100 times?
starter: A task repeats exactly five times. Would a counter or an unknown stopping condition be clearer?
starter_answer: A count-controlled loop is suitable because the number of repetitions is known.
terms: A variable used to build a running total.

stations.name: Repeat a known count
facts: Use a count-controlled loop for a known count.
Be clear whether the last value is included.
OCR for loops include their stated end value.
stations.challenge: How many times does this loop print?
stations.answer: Three times, because 1, 2 and 3 are included.

tasks.q: OCR pseudocode: for i = 1 to 4. How many iterations?
OCR for i = 2 to 5 executes...
tasks.fb: 4 times. Use a count-controlled loop for a known count.

stations.info: Three times, because 1, 2 and 3 are included.

stations.name: Repeat until a condition
facts: A while loop checks before its body.
It can execute zero times.
The condition must eventually become false.
stations.challenge: When does the loop stop?
stations.answer: When count becomes 3, count < 3 is false.

tasks.q: A while condition is false before the first check. How often does its body run?
tasks.fb: Zero times

tasks.q: Which loop can execute zero times?
a: A loop fixed at three repetitions
tasks.fb: A while loop. A while loop checks before its body.

stations.info: When count becomes 3, count < 3 is false.

stations.name: Accumulate a total
facts: Set a starting total before the loop.
Add each new value to the running total.
Do not reset the total during each iteration.
stations.challenge: What goes wrong if total = 0 is inside the loop?
stations.answer: Earlier values are discarded at each iteration, so the running total is lost.

tasks.q: Starting at 0, add 5, 2 and 8. What is the total?
Where should a running total normally be initialised?
tasks.fb: Before the loop. Set a starting total before the loop.

stations.info: Earlier values are discarded at each iteration, so the running total is lost.

stations.name: Guarantee progress
facts: A loop needs a way to reach its stopping case.
Update the control variable correctly.
Trace the update and condition together.
stations.challenge: What happens if the update is removed?
stations.answer: x stays 0, so x < 3 remains true and the loop does not terminate.

tasks.q: What fixes a loop whose counter never changes?
a: Update the counter towards the stopping condition
tasks.fb: Update the counter towards the stopping condition

tasks.q: x = 0, while x < 3, x = x + 1. Final x?
tasks.fb: 3. A loop needs a way to reach its stopping case.

stations.info: x stays 0, so x < 3 remains true and the loop does not terminate.

stations.name: Selection inside a loop
facts: A loop can repeat a decision.
The decision runs for each item.
Only matching items affect the count.
stations.challenge: How many of 2, 7, 8 and 3 are at least 7?
stations.answer: Two values: 7 and 8.

tasks.q: Which values pass value >= 5 in [1, 5, 8]?
tasks.fb: 5 and 8

tasks.q: Count values > 5 in [5, 6, 2, 8]. Count?
tasks.fb: 2. A loop can repeat a decision.

stations.info: Two values: 7 and 8.

stations.name: Nested loops
facts: An inner loop runs for each outer iteration.
Count repetitions at both levels.
Multiply fixed counts when both fully execute.
stations.challenge: How many prints for outer 4 and inner 3?
stations.answer: Twelve prints: the three inner iterations run for each of four outer iterations.

tasks.q: Outer loop runs twice. Inner loop runs five times each time. Total inner executions?
Outer 3, inner 4, both fixed counts. Inner runs?
tasks.fb: 12. An inner loop runs for each outer iteration.

stations.info: Twelve prints: the three inner iterations run for each of four outer iterations.

final.q: Order a running-total algorithm.
steps: Add the value to total inside the loop
final.fb: Initialise once, update repeatedly and output at the end.

final.q: A loop starts n = 1, adds 1 while n < 4. What is n after the loop?

plenary: Explain one difference between count-controlled and condition-controlled loops. [2]
Count-controlled repetition uses a specified count/range (1). Condition-controlled repetition depends on a condition (1).
Write pseudocode to input three numbers and output their total. [4]
Initialise total (1), loop exactly three times (1), input and add each value (1), output total after the loop (1).
Why might a while loop never terminate? [2]
Its condition remains true (1), for example because the control variable is never updated (1).
practical: In Python, write and run a program that inputs three numbers and prints their total. Test 2, 3, 4 (expected 9) and -2, 2, 0 (expected 0).

title: Linear search depot
subject: Linear search
mission: Search equipment records one at a time. Trace successful and unsuccessful linear searches.
donow: How would you find an item in a box with no useful ordering?
starter: Search [18, 4, 27, 9] from left to right for 27. Which values are checked?
starter_answer: 18, then 4, then 27. Stop when 27 is found.
terms: Checking items one at a time until a target is found or the list ends.
A position used to access an item in a list.

stations.name: Check one at a time
facts: Start at the first item.
Compare the item with the target.
Continue if it does not match.
stations.challenge: How many target comparisons find 27?
stations.answer: Three comparisons. With zero-based indexing, its index is 2.

tasks.q: Order a successful search for 27 in [18, 4, 27, 9].
tasks.fb: Do not continue checking after the first match in this version.

tasks.q: Search [8, 6, 4] for 8. Comparisons?
tasks.fb: 1. Start at the first item.

stations.info: Three comparisons. With zero-based indexing, its index is 2.

stations.name: Unsorted lists
facts: Linear search does not need sorted data.
Every item is still checked in sequence.
It also works on sorted lists.
stations.challenge: Why can linear search use an unsorted list?
